## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered}

A street vendor earns different amount per day, so we have (e1, ... e30).
We can plot that data, day on x axis and value on y axis, we will have sticks with different height.
Another way to visualize is to add daily earnings so we have stairs (of different height). day 1 is e1, day 2 is e1 + e2, day 3 is e1 + e2 + e3.

There is no better or worse way, it is in fact the same data.
The stair which is what is called cumulative is better to answer for instance how much one earns after one week, 2 weeks etc and eventually monthly earning.
But it is completely useless if you want to calculate the mean daily earning or the max earning.

The new object is simply a different way of visualizing a distribution @sec-distribution. Whereas one can reveal  @sec-mean, @sec-mode for a cumulative is mostly used to look at quantile @sec-median and @sec-quantile.

This is a just a different way of looking a distribution.
It only applies for quantitative variable.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
In advanced mathematical statistics, textbooks clarify a common terminological distinction before providing rigorous definitions:
Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) is the unifying, mathematically precise term for the "cumulative density and mass distribution" of any random variable.
Probability Mass Function (PMF) applies strictly to discrete variables.
Probability Density Function (PDF) applies strictly to continuous variables.

Here are the rigorous definitions from two universally cited textbooks in mathematical statistics.

1. The Unifying Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)
The CDF completely determines the probability distribution of a random variable, regardless of whether it is discrete or continuous.

Textbook Source
Book: Statistical Inference (2nd Edition, 2002)
Authors: George Casella and Roger L. Berger
Publisher: Duxbury / Thomson Learning

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability Theory"), Casella and Berger define the cumulative distribution function of a random variable X:
Definition 1.5.1: "The cumulative distribution function of a random variable X, denoted by FX(x), is defined by

$F_X(x) = P_X(X \le x), \quad \text{for all } x.$

[...] The abbreviation cdf will be used to denote cumulative distribution function."


Rigorous Mathematical Properties of a CDF
For FX(x) to be a valid cumulative distribution function, it must satisfy three rigorous mathematical properties:


1.Monotonicity: It is nondecreasing; if x $x_1 < x_2 \implies F_X(x_1) \le F_X(x_2)$

2. Limits: $\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to \infty} F_X(x) = 1$

3. Continuity: It is right-continuous; for every x $\lim_{x \to x_0^+} F_X(x) = F_X(x_0)$


1. The Discrete Case: Probability Mass Function (PMF)
When dealing with a discrete variable, the cumulative distribution accumulates point probabilities.

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019)
Authors: Robert V. Hogg, Joseph W. McKean, and Allen T. Craig
Publisher: Pearson

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability and Distributions"), Hogg, McKean, and Craig formalize the discrete case:
"Let X be a discrete random variable with space D. The probability mass function (pmf) of X is defined by

$p_X(x) = P(X = x), \quad \text{for } x \in \mathcal{D}$


and pX(x)=0 otherwise."

The Mass Distribution Relation
The cumulative mass distribution is achieved by summing these discrete points up to a value x:

$F_X(x) = \sum_{x_i \le x} p_X(x_i)$

1. The Continuous Case: Probability Density Function (PDF)
When dealing with a continuous variable, probability at a single point is zero, requiring calculus to evaluate a cumulative range.

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019) — Same Source

The Definition
Hogg, McKean, and Craig define the continuous random variable and its underlying density function:
"We say a random variable X is a continuous random variable if its cumulative distribution function FX(x) is continuous for all x∈R. [...] The probability density function (pdf) of X is a function fX(x) such that

$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) \, dt$
for all x∈R.


By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, at points where fX
(x) is continuous,
$f_X(x) = \frac{d}{dx}F_X(x)$."

The Density Distribution Relation

The cumulative density distribution is achieved by integrating the density function:
$P(a \le X \le b) = \int_{a}^{b} f_X(x) \, dx = F_X(b) - F_X(a)$

Conceptual Summary
"Mass" (PMF): Used for countable outcomes. The cumulative mass function looks like a stair-step graph because probability jumps up only at distinct, specific numbers.
"Density" (PDF): Used for continuous measurements. The cumulative density function is a smooth, unbroken curve because probability is spread continuously over an interval of real numbers.
